findings.description: Carried from r5 and r6, unchanged. The `echo ` and `require_text` exclusions still drop real invocations written on those lines, and I reproduced the resulting false PASS. It stays minor because the trigger requires an idiom the suite does not use anywhere, on top of the misplacement the bound exists to catch.
findings.evidence: constitution.md:465-467 for the exclusions, :477 for the explanation. New artifact R: banner and binding inside the guard with `require_file "$stamper"` as the only in-bounds use, and both real invocations appended after the comparison as `echo "$(bash "$stamper" ...)"`. Result: 'snap=587 banner=1297 bind=1298 first-use=1299 last-use=1299 cmp=1304' -> 'inside the guard'. That is the clause's own failing example at :519 going green again. What holds it below the r6 blocker's bar: `echo "$(...)"` is a useless-use-of-echo that appears nowhere in the 1309-line suite, whose actual capture idiom is `out="$(bash "$migrator" ...)"` — which the block counts correctly — so no worker following house style lands here, and no checker running the block on a normally-written section decides differently. The clause still owes the worker one sentence turning the exclusions into a rule: invoke the stamper on a plain `bash "$stamper" ...` line or capture it into a variable, never inside an `echo` or a `require_text`. Two adjacent behaviors I probed and am not filing: a duplicate `^stamper=` binding (artifact S) makes the test emit '[: 1298|1301: integer expression expected' and print OUTSIDE, and an indented binding (artifact T) leaves bind empty and prints OUTSIDE. Both fail safe, both toward a false FAIL with a legible signal.

findings.description: New, and the weakest of the six. The contract's sort key is not falsified by any check — only the order-stability it exists to produce is. A stamper that sorts output lines by whole line rather than by path satisfies every check in the document.
findings.evidence: constitution.md:73, 'Lines come out sorted by resolved record path, never in argument order'. My reference stamper's final `printf '%s' "$lines" | sort` sorts whole lines, so 'skipped:' sorts before 'stamped:' regardless of path — C-2 printed the decisions record before the context one, the reverse of r6's reference stamper. It still passed C-1 through C-7 and C-18 verbatim, order-independence included. Filed as a minor rather than a finding because the property the clause argues for at :73 — 'a report that reshuffles between two runs over the same inbox is a report nobody can diff' — is fully delivered by either sort, C-5's arity-2 comparison falsifies the argument-order implementation the rule is aimed at, and no checker would decide differently. If it is ever tightened, the cheap fix is an anchored expected-output line in C-18 rather than new prose.

findings.description: The two-stage rule and its six-row branch table are exhaustive, ordered and mutually exclusive. I implemented the table literally, in bash 3.2 with parallel indexed arrays, and it satisfied C-1 through C-7 and C-18 without a special case.
findings.evidence: constitution.md:77-93 for the rule and table. Stage 1 collapses to one candidate per realpath taking the max note date; stage 2 walks the six rows in order. The 3.2 warning at :46 is real and correctly scoped — the keyed max-date dedupe is the only thing in the job that wants an associative array, and a linear scan over parallel arrays does it. The all-or-nothing validation rule at :105 is what forces the parse-everything-then-decide shape; a streaming implementation cannot satisfy it. I could not make stage 1 and stage 2 disagree: stage 1 never reads record state, and the budget outcome is date-independent because every ISO date is ten characters and the inserted line count is one.
